The record lacks mesh type/position, collection accessibility, fistula assessment and prior source-control attempts needed to compare salvage, drainage and explantation. Do not infer that explantation is necessarily wrong or necessarily mandatory.
Importance: high. Realism: plausible for an abdominal-wall clinic.
Too easy: cautious referral beats caricatured repeat treatment and a prejudged fixed operation.
suggestions: Choose one decision stage: either compare specific investigations for the persistent sinus or provide sufficient operative/source-control data to compare actual treatments.
Remove 'as the fixed plan' and make all alternatives sound like real proposals.
Name the concrete action in the key and obtain clinician adjudication of salvage versus explantation under the supplied circumstances.

title: Nutrition composition in a proven leak

cues.phrase: The prescribed calories and protein are achieved by mouth.
cues.why: Explicitly eliminates the calorie-increase alternative and favors preserving the oral route.

cues.phrase: Listed fat source: long-chain triglycerides.
cues.why: Names the component changed only by the key; the task can be solved by ingredient matching.

cues.phrase: Use low long-chain-fat intake with medium-chain-fat enrichment
cues.why: Only choice specifies nutrient composition and contains both the implicated ingredient and its proposed replacement.

cues.phrase: Stable fluid and electrolyte management, no sepsis or enteral intolerance.
cues.why: Supplies a list of permissions for the diet option while making PN appear excessive.

fairness: A fat-composition change is a plausible initial nutritional measure, but 'output remains substantial' is not a usable description of leak severity or trajectory.

The record does not establish duration, prior dietary measures or consequences of ongoing loss. PN can be a credible leak-management strategy despite adequate oral calories; oral tolerance alone does not resolve the comparison.
Importance: useful postoperative nutrition knowledge; moderate frequency in general surgery. Realism: home management of a substantial ongoing leak needs clearer monitoring and specialist context.
Too easy by wording; the missing severity information creates uncertainty, not legitimate additional difficulty.
suggestions: Give supported output trajectory, nutritional consequences and duration of attempted treatment, without inventing an escalation threshold.
Compare specific nutrition strategies at the same stage, and have the clinician verify when the represented leak favors diet modification over PN.
Remove adequacy summaries and use relevant delivery data; keep the actual supplement composition but make its interpretation necessary rather than a word-match answer.

title: Hereditary testing sequence

cues.phrase: No inherited variant has yet been identified in Miriam.
cues.why: Logically rules out targeted testing for a known familial variant without requiring interpretation of the IHC panel.

cues.phrase: Colon tumor tissue, not a constitutional blood sample.
cues.why: Preteaches the tumor-versus-germline distinction the learner is supposed to apply.

cues.phrase: Repeat the same tumor IHC as the family test
cues.why: 'As the family test' advertises a category mistake; repeating the same tumor test is an implausible family-testing plan.

cues.phrase: before Miriam has any further tests.
cues.why: The request explicitly contrasts testing the unaffected relative first with the keyed affected-patient workup.

fairness: Affected-patient genetic counseling/germline assessment is a defensible pathway; an abnormal tumor screen is not itself a named familial germline variant.
Importance: high for colorectal cancer and family-risk care. Realism: credible clinic question, but the distractor's targeted-test request is engineered to be impossible.
Too easy: the key follows without reading which mismatch-repair proteins are lost; the detailed IHC is decorative.
suggestions: Make the specific IHC pattern determine a real next test in the affected patient, comparing credible reflex/germline pathways with supported criteria.
Alternatively give an actual verified familial finding and ask a consequential relative-testing decision.
Remove the tumor-not-blood teaching clause and avoid a distractor that proposes an explicitly nonexistent target.

title: Changed gastric lymphoma tissue

cues.phrase: New enlarging ulcerated mass; multiple samples show broad sheets of large atypical B cells replacing the previous small-cell architecture.
cues.why: The emphatic old-versus-new contrast makes unchanged observation unattractive even without classifying the pathology.

cues.phrase: Appropriately timed nonserologic test remains negative after the documented medication washout.
cues.why: An author-certified valid negative rules out the repeat-eradication option; 'appropriately' replaces the data needed to judge validity.

cues.phrase: Hematology review of staging and lymphoma-directed therapy
cues.why: Only comprehensive specialist-escalation package competes against an explicitly unsupported infection treatment and passive observation.

fairness: A new large-cell process warrants hematopathology/staging review; the supplied description supports concern but this review does not independently certify a precise transformed lymphoma diagnosis.
The key does not name actual treatment; 'lymphoma-directed therapy' cannot be compared meaningfully with the specific eradication proposal.
Importance: moderate; a useful recognition of changed gastric lymphoma biology, though definitive systemic therapy is a hematology decision. Realism: plausible surgical/foregut follow-up.
Too easy as offered: worsening cancer plus negative infection testing selects the only oncology escalation, without the pathology needing to change a concrete plan.
suggestions: Ask for a specific next staging/tissue-confirmation action, or supply definitive classification and enough staging context for a concrete treatment comparison.
Replace 'appropriately timed' and 'documented medication washout' with the actual relevant record if infection-test validity affects the answer.
Use credible lymphoma pathways at the same stage rather than retreatment and observation foils.

title: Pleural drainage despite partial response
fairness: A defensible best answer is initial intercostal tube drainage: the learner must interpret the pleural-fluid findings despite systemic improvement, then select an initial drainage approach rather than observation or immediate operative drainage.

The options are parallel pleural-management actions. Nonpurulent appearance and improving systemic measures provide a credible observation temptation; operative drainage is a plausible escalation error.

The analyzed sample conditions and accessible pocket are decision-critical validity/feasibility data, not an unfair unique-key permission: they do not by themselves choose tube drainage over the other plans. Do not remove them merely to make the item harder.

Importance: high; pleural source control is practical general-surgery knowledge. Realism: acceptable as a documented hospital-team consultation reviewed in clinic, with drainage implemented through acute hospital care, not an ordinary delayed clinic procedure.
PASS is editorial for these visible fields, not clinician approval or an independent verification of a numerical guideline threshold. A new threshold is not asserted here.
suggestions: Preserve the systemic-versus-pleural discordance and balanced management options.
Make the hospital consultation/implementation pathway clear in encounter integration; do not permit the clinic wrapper to imply routine delayed follow-up for the keyed drainage plan.

title: Standby treatment and emergency action

cues.phrase: the illness has not been examined by a clinician.
cues.why: Announces the omitted assessment and directs the solver to the only immediate assessment option.

cues.phrase: no clinician has assessed this illness or established its cause.
cues.why: Repeats the same named omission in a second exhibit row.

cues.phrase: Proceed to immediate hospital emergency assessment today
cues.why: Only option offers prompt assessment of an explicitly unassessed, still-weak febrile patient; both distractors advertise delay.

fairness: Immediate emergency assessment is defensible in the represented asplenic febrile illness. Do not remove fever/chills or other safety findings to create artificial difficulty.
Importance: high and practically important. Realism: a telephone call to the surgical clinic is credible.

Too easy for a difficult resident item: standard safety recognition with repeated direction to an uncompleted assessment. The standby antibiotic and antipyretic response do not create a difficult second decision.
suggestions: Seek explicit acceptance as a safety-recognition exception, keeping the urgent action clear.
If a Level 3/4 item is needed, move to a concrete subsequent care decision with the necessary observations and credible competing plans.
Delete duplicate no-clinician-yet statements; give the actual call timeline and current symptoms once.

title: Meal adaptation and vascular symptoms

cues.phrase: a normal-sized meal still produces the prior pain.
cues.why: Explicitly resolves the claimed symptom improvement as food avoidance rather than leaving the learner to infer it from the diary.

cues.phrase: Endoscopy and other evaluation have not identified an alternative cause matching the course.
cues.why: Blanket diagnostic exclusion removes competing explanations without showing the relevant findings.

cues.phrase: Significant occlusive disease of both the celiac and superior mesenteric arteries.
cues.why: An interpreted significance label supplies the vascular conclusion and directly matches the only vascular treatment option.

fairness: Vascular revascularization planning is a defensible direction in the represented syndrome. The item does not need an invented stenosis cutoff to make that point.

Importance: high; recognizing food avoidance despite reported improvement is consequential. Realism: plausible outpatient reassessment if no acute deterioration, which the examination appropriately addresses.

Too easy with these alternatives: normal-meal pain, weight loss, interpreted multivessel disease and blanket exclusion overwhelm a nutrition-only plan. 'Functional ischemia testing' is also not a specifically named test.
The intended two steps could be valid, but the first is largely supplied and no meaningful intervention choice follows.
suggestions: Use actual meal/weight chronology and relevant imaging observations without the interpretive 'significant' or blanket alternative-exclusion statements.
Compare concrete diagnostic or revascularization pathways at one stage, with supported findings distinguishing the nearest competitor.
Keep the safety assessment and make the food-adaptation interpretation change a specific action.

title: Head injury decision-rule scope

cues.phrase: A clinic triage worksheet is the only completed assessment.
cues.why: Frames the reassuring assessment as incomplete and points toward the only hospital reassessment plan.

cues.phrase: Hospital assessment with head computed tomography strongly considered
cues.why: The key is uniquely cautious and flexible; the other options commit to no imaging or waiting for deterioration.

cues.phrase: head computed tomography after deterioration
cues.why: Advertises delayed response as the competing plan, making it easy to reject without knowing rule eligibility.

fairness: The unnamed 'usual mild-head-injury rule' cannot be audited for applicability or a valid low-risk result. The patient's age and absence of reported loss of consciousness may matter differently under different rules; this review cannot certify the worksheet conclusion.
Hospital assessment with imaging consideration is a defensible direction in this anticoagulated head-impact scenario, but 'strongly considered' is not a concrete imaging decision.
Importance: high as trauma safety. Realism: an incidental injury at an unrelated clinic visit is possible, but is a wrapper rather than a surgical-clinic management problem.
Too easy by cautious-option selection; ambiguity about the rule must not be counted as difficulty.
suggestions: Name the actual validated rule and show the relevant inputs/eligibility instead of 'usual' and 'low risk'; obtain clinician verification of its scope.
Choose one concrete task: disposition or imaging. Phrase all options with equal decisiveness.
If the objective remains anticoagulant safety recognition, seek explicit basic/safety acceptance instead of claiming two-step reasoning.

title: Discordant cardiac screening

cues.phrase: Above this assay's upper reference limit
cues.why: The only abnormal screening result makes the moderate monitoring option stand out against discharge and invasive support.

cues.phrase: Stable circulation; no other injury explains a need for intensive care.
cues.why: An explicit exclusion pre-dismisses the invasive-support distractor.

cues.phrase: Monitoring decision was not completed before the clinic review.
cues.why: Names the omitted decision that the key supplies.

cues.phrase: Admission for invasive hemodynamic support
cues.why: An extreme escalation has no represented hemodynamic indication and makes routine monitored care the obvious middle option.

fairness: Hospital monitoring is a defensible disposition for the discordant screening findings. Troponin elevation should not be silently treated as a complete diagnosis of the cause of injury.

Importance: high in trauma training. Realism: an ED patient with an unresolved abnormal cardiac screen being routed to outpatient clinic is questionable unless this is explicitly a real-time consult or retrospective record review.
Too easy: one abnormal result plus an extreme ICU foil; no consequential second inference.
suggestions: Clarify the active acute-care setting and include test timing, symptoms and relevant baseline context if they affect interpretation.
Compare credible monitoring, repeat-testing or additional-cardiac-evaluation plans rather than unsupported invasive support.
Remove the named missing-monitoring sentence and let the actual screen determine the disposition.

title: Chest injury monitoring endpoint

cues.phrase: documented that the fracture can be managed without admission.
cues.why: Preapproves outpatient management before the cardiac data are interpreted.

cues.phrase: Stable circulation, manageable pain and no other reason for hospital admission.
cues.why: Broadly states the no-admission rationale and makes both admission alternatives sound unsupported.

cues.phrase: Unmonitored ward admission after the completed assessment
cues.why: For a task specifically about additional cardiac care, this offers neither a cardiac intervention nor a stated noncardiac indication.

fairness: The normal ECG/troponin combination supports the intended outpatient cardiac disposition in an appropriately completed assessment; this offline review does not establish a universal sampling timetable.

'Completed troponin I' does not give injury-to-sampling chronology. If acquisition timing determines whether the screen is complete, that information should be visible rather than certified by the adjective.
Importance: high for avoiding unnecessary trauma admission. Realism: an outside record review is possible, but a same-episode disposition decision belongs in the acute-care workflow.
Too easy: all represented findings are reassuring and both foils admit without a supported indication.
suggestions: Provide the actual testing chronology and relevant eligibility observations without global no-admission conclusions.
Compare credible discharge versus monitoring plans that hinge on a meaningful test-completion or symptom issue.
If retaining the isolated-sternal-fracture rule, identify it as a basic screening endpoint rather than a difficult two-step item.

title: Ventilation after fluid-weight change

cues.phrase: Fixed measurements
cues.why: The row heading preclassifies the desired invariant inputs.

cues.phrase: Adult height and recorded sex unchanged throughout the admission.
cues.why: Directly describes the stable anthropometric inputs used only by the keyed calculation.

cues.phrase: Predicted body weight from the documented anthropometric calculation
cues.why: The key is the uniquely technical calculated measure; the two distractors both use actual scale weights that the stem has already portrayed as fluid-dependent.

cues.phrase: A note proposes recalculating the weight basis from each day's scale reading.
cues.why: Rehearses the specific wrong practice, making rejection of current actual weight obvious.

fairness: Predicted body weight is a defensible basis for the represented ARDS prescription; this report adds no numerical ventilation target.

Importance: high in general-surgery critical care. Realism: retrospective postoperative/ICU review is possible, but deciding a ventilator weight basis in a clinic conversation is artificial unless explicitly educational case review.
Too easy: a single foundational ventilation rule; fluid variation adds narrative but does not create a second consequential step.
The exhibit gives no actual height or weight values to interpret, so its table-like structure does not increase cognitive demand.
suggestions: Use an actual supported ventilator record requiring interpretation of the prescription and selection of a concrete adjustment, with relevant patient measurements and respiratory constraints.
Do not simply add arithmetic unless it changes a consequential decision; compare credible ventilator plans.
Alternatively seek explicit acceptance as foundational ICU knowledge and remove the decorative clinic/fixed-measurements framing.

title: Incidental stones during abdominal workup

cues.phrase: no prior upper-abdominal attacks or meal-related right-sided pain.
cues.why: Explicitly excludes the symptomatic gallbladder rationale for the cholecystectomy option.

cues.phrase: Sigmoid inflammation matched the painful site
cues.why: Provides the symptom-attribution conclusion instead of leaving localization to the learner.

cues.phrase: No special high-risk gallbladder circumstance is documented.
cues.why: A blanket eligibility/exclusion statement preempts exceptions without giving the underlying observations.

cues.phrase: Therapeutic ERCP for the gallbladder stones
cues.why: An anatomically mismatched treatment label is a weak resident distractor; no ductal problem is represented.

fairness: Observation is defensible for the represented incidental asymptomatic stones, but the blanket high-risk exclusion is not a clinical assessment a learner can independently evaluate.
Importance: high; avoiding surgery for incidental findings is practical. Realism: credible surgical-clinic counseling.
Too easy: the symptom cause is already assigned and both alternatives intervene on an explicitly asymptomatic finding.
suggestions: Provide a symptom chronology requiring genuine attribution rather than explicitly declaring the CT matched the pain.
Use credible competing gallbladder plans and any specific patient factors necessary to rank them; omit a ductal intervention unless ductal disease is truly a competing concern.
Delete the unspecific no-high-risk-circumstance declaration; supply only decision-relevant supported facts.

title: Venous treatment eligibility

cues.phrase: He wants procedural treatment.
cues.why: States the intervention preference before any interpretation.

cues.phrase: Suitable anatomy and general condition for specialist superficial-vein intervention assessment.
cues.why: The author supplies procedural eligibility as a conclusion.

cues.phrase: Understands conservative and procedural approaches and prefers intervention.
cues.why: Repeats the preference and supplies informed-choice permission for the key.

cues.phrase: before any superficial venous intervention referral
cues.why: 'Any' makes the competing stocking requirement categorical rather than a realistic individualized proposal.

cues.phrase: Observation until a skin complication warrants another review
cues.why: Advertises withholding reassessment despite current symptoms, making the referral key the only responsive plan.

fairness: Referral for intervention discussion can be defensible without an arbitrary mandatory stocking trial, but this offline review has not verified a current guideline or payer policy.
Importance: useful vascular-clinic practice. Realism: plausible referral barrier, provided clinical guidance and administrative coverage requirements are not conflated.
The key says 'intervention referral' rather than a named procedure; it is an assessment pathway competing against treatment prerequisites, not a definitive treatment selection.
Too easy: eligibility and preference are supplied repeatedly; the task is mainly recall of a no-mandatory-trial rule.
suggestions: Ask specifically about referral eligibility or supply actual anatomy for a named treatment decision; do not mix these stages.
Describe relevant duplex and medical observations rather than 'suitable', and state preference once.
Use credible conservative and procedural plans without absolute barriers or waiting for complications as a straw alternative.

title: Changed post-repair pain assessment

cues.phrase: Deep ache accompanies a visible contour during cough or lifting and eases when the contour reduces.
cues.why: Mechanism language maps directly to the only dynamic local test; the key can be chosen by location and motion matching.

cues.phrase: A repeat nerve procedure is booked using the earlier pain diagnosis.
cues.why: Prelabels the existing plan as based on stale information and directs the solver away from the repeat block.

cues.phrase: Lumbar MRI as the next pain investigation
cues.why: The distant-site study has no represented spinal or radicular findings and is not a credible close alternative.

fairness: Dynamic assessment of possible recurrent hernia is defensible, and the question correctly avoids treating a negative supine examination as proof against a dynamic lesion.

A standing cough/Valsalva examination is not documented. The key should not silently imply imaging must precede an adequate dynamic clinical examination; clarify what was actually attempted and remained uncertain.
Importance: high. Realism: clinically plausible for a postoperative hernia clinic.
Too easy with these choices: the changed local bulge selects local dynamic imaging, while neither alternative assesses the new physical finding.
suggestions: Supply the actual dynamic examination findings and residual uncertainty that justify imaging.
Compare credible local assessment or imaging pathways rather than lumbar imaging unsupported by symptoms.
Preserve the distinction between the earlier neuropathic pain and new mechanical symptoms, but let the observations establish it without labelling the scheduled plan stale.

title: Skin-cancer risk beyond size

cues.phrase: routine low-risk excision because the visible lesion is small.
cues.why: Frames the referral's reasoning as an obvious one-feature oversimplification.

cues.phrase: poor differentiation.
cues.why: An adverse-sounding histology label directly contradicts the 'low-risk' distractor even without interpreting perineural involvement.

cues.phrase: Routine low-risk standard excision planning
cues.why: The distractor advertises low risk against an exhibit specifically emphasizing adverse pathology.

cues.phrase: Clinical observation after the diagnostic biopsy
cues.why: Offers no treatment for explicitly invasive cancer and becomes a nonfunctioning distractor.

fairness: A margin-controlled/Mohs assessment is defensible for the adverse cutaneous squamous findings; the record does not establish that every alternative standard excision strategy would be wrong.

'Small' is not an actual measurement, and site, depth, nerve features and clinical neurological findings may matter to the fuller high-risk plan. Do not imply Mohs assessment exhausts all needed evaluation.
Importance: high for skin surgery; perineural involvement can materially alter planning. Realism: plausible clinic referral, but the options evade a real comparison of acceptable surgical strategies.
Too easy: risk-label contradiction selects the only escalated surgical assessment; two pathological observations do not by themselves make two-step reasoning.
suggestions: Give measured lesion/site and relevant biopsy findings, then compare concrete margin-management or staging pathways at the same stage.
Remove the 'low-risk' judgement from the distractor and replace observation with a credible competing operation/evaluation.
Have the clinician adjudicate which supplied feature makes the selected pathway preferable, and preserve any additional staging uncertainty.

cues.why: Announces the missing information and steers to the only new local anatomical study.

cues.phrase: local report does not define sphincter and adjacent pelvic involvement.
cues.why: Explicitly supplies the MRI-selection rationale, including key-only pelvic wording.

cues.phrase: Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen and pelvis
cues.why: Repeats the already completed study without a different protocol or question.

cues.phrase: Repeat superficial biopsy of the anal lesion
cues.why: Repeats a completed diagnostic category and adds 'superficial', advertising inadequacy for the requested local extent.

cues.why: Decorative attachment adds no staging evidence and repeats the key's anatomical word rather than creating a plausible comparison.

suggestions: Remove the unrelated hip radiograph and the explanatory 'superficial' qualifier.

Compare credible local/regional staging studies with a specific patient/anatomical uncertainty that distinguishes their roles, or supply actual staging findings and ask the consequential treatment-planning step.
Use a neutral complete task and avoid merely filling the missing test named by the stem.
